faq.a: Hypertension is a maternal cause; insufficiency is the resulting fetal condition. Both can coexist, and treating hypertension may improve placental flow.
faq.q: How does placental insufficiency differ from maternal hypertension?

exam: What bedside findings would prompt you to order an umbilical artery Doppler? — Lagging fundal height, maternal hypertension, or known infection; Doppler assesses placental resistance.
A 32‑week pregnant woman with malaria and fundal height 4 cm behind dates. What is your next step? — Treat malaria, repeat fundal measurement in 2 weeks, arrange ultrasound to assess growth.
Explain why reversed end‑diastolic flow on Doppler mandates delivery even at 30 weeks. — It indicates severe placental resistance and fetal hypoxia, outweighing prematurity risks.

How would you differentiate fetal growth restriction due to placental insufficiency from a constitutional small baby? — Compare growth curves, assess Doppler, and look for maternal risk factors; constitutional smallness has normal Doppler.
Why are ACE inhibitors contraindicated in a pregnant woman with hypertension? — They cause fetal renal dysgenesis and oligohydramnios, worsening placental insufficiency.
In a low‑resource clinic without Doppler, how would you monitor a suspected case? — Serial fundal height, maternal weight gain, symptom review, and timely referral for ultrasound if available.
What maternal condition most commonly co‑exists with placental insufficiency in East Africa? — Chronic anemia and malaria infection.

Describe the management plan for a 36‑week fetus with absent end‑diastolic flow but stable heart rate. — Counsel for immediate delivery (induction or cesarean), give steroids if <34 weeks, monitor maternal vitals.
ai.title: Placental Insufficiency
ai.subject: Obstetrics & gynaecology
ai.summary: Placental insufficiency is reduced placental blood flow causing fetal growth restriction and distress. It is diagnosed by clinical, ultrasound and Doppler findings, and managed by monitoring and timely delivery.

b: Most common cause of late‑term IUGR
Higher prevalence in low‑resource settings with maternal anemia, infection, and hypertension
sections.p: Placental insufficiency occurs when the placenta cannot deliver adequate oxygen and nutrients to the fetus, leading to intra‑uterine growth restriction (IUGR) and possible stillbirth.

b: Umbilical artery pulsatility index >95th percentile = abnormal resistance
Maternal hypertension, anemia, malaria, HIV, TB, and malnutrition are common precipitants
sections.p: The problem is at the level of the uteroplacental circulation. Severity is staged by fetal growth percentiles and Doppler waveforms.

b: Fundal height lag >2 cm behind dates warrants ultrasound
Persistent abnormal Doppler predicts poor outcome
Early delivery balances prematurity against intra‑uterine demise
sections.p: Patients may be asymptomatic; diagnosis relies on antenatal visits, fundal height measurement, and targeted ultrasound. Untreated severe insufficiency can cause fetal hypoxia, acidosis, and death.
When Doppler is unavailable, rely on serial fundal height and growth scans; consider early delivery if growth falls off trend.

t.b: Is fetal growth tracking appropriately? A lag >2 cm suggests growth restriction.
What is the estimated fetal weight? Weight <10th percentile confirms IUGR.
Is placental resistance high? Elevated PI or absent/reversed end‑diastolic flow indicates severe insufficiency.

t.a: Maternal blood pressure and urine protein
t.b: Is pre‑eclampsia present? Hypertension with proteinuria suggests a maternal contribution.

t.a: Maternal hemoglobin, malaria smear, HIV test
t.b: Are treatable infections or anemia present? Positive results guide specific therapy.

b: Control hypertension with labetalol or methyldopa; avoid ACE inhibitors
Treat malaria with ACT, anemia with iron/folate, HIV with ART
Serial ultrasounds every 2‑4 weeks; Doppler weekly if abnormal
Delivery: <34 weeks – give steroids, consider cesarean if Doppler shows reversed flow; ≥34 weeks – induce labor if fetal status stable
sections.p: Treat underlying maternal conditions, provide close fetal surveillance, and plan delivery based on gestational age and severity.

b: Ask about malaria episodes, HIV status, and nutrition
Check for signs of pre‑eclampsia (headache, visual changes, edema)
Know that absent end‑diastolic flow is an indication for delivery regardless of gestational age
sections.p: Focus on pattern recognition: small fundal height, abnormal Doppler, and maternal risk factors. Remember that in low‑resource settings, clinical assessment may be the only tool.

b: Assuming a single fundal‑height lag rules out IUGR – need serial measurements
Delaying delivery when Doppler shows reversed flow – risk of fetal death
Ignoring maternal anemia or malaria, which can improve placental perfusion when treated
sections.p: Errors often arise from over‑reliance on a single measurement or missing treatable maternal causes.

whenToSeekHelp: Maternal hypertension with severe headache or visual disturbance
Fetal heart rate decelerations or absent movements
Rapidly worsening Doppler findings (reversed end‑diastolic flow)
